title: Carrier-mediated spin helices in low-dimensional systems: Josephson-interference features and correlation renormalization
abstract: Carrier-induced helical magnetism can arise in interacting one-dimensional systems coupled to localized moments. Here, we investigate the coupled-wire sliding-Luttinger-liquid counterparts with and without valley degrees of freedom, using isolated Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids as reference limits. The carrier spin susceptibility mediates a Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida interaction that selects the helical ordering wave vector, while interchannel correlations lock the relative helix phases and stabilize a collective quasi-two-dimensional texture. Using a variational treatment, we estimate the helix-induced partial gap and analyze the reconstruction of the remaining gapless carrier modes. To probe the spatial texture through transport, we incorporate the helix into an anisotropic superconductor-normal-metal-superconductor Josephson junction motivated by the coupled-channel structure of twisted bilayer WTe$_2$. We exploit flux focusing near the junction interfaces to make an applied in-plane field a controlled probe of the spin helix. Relative to junctions without the helix, the helical exchange field modifies the central-lobe width and relative lobe weights. In the transverse-channel geometry, it also produces field-dependent side-lobe asymmetry and central-peak displacement, which remain negligible in the matched references for the parameters considered. The reconstructed carrier sector also exhibits modified local-density-of-states exponents, spin-relaxation behavior, and competing correlations, with distinct signatures in isolated and coupled-wire systems. Our results connect collective helical order in coupled-wire systems to carrier-sector reconstruction and identify field-tunable Josephson interferometry as a complementary transport probe of the spatial spin texture.
summary: This work theoretically explores how spin helicity, mediated by itinerant carriers interacting with localized moments, establishes collective magnetic order in low-dimensional conductors. The authors predict that this helical order leaves distinct, measurable fingerprints in the Josephson current interference patterns and modifies the electronic structure of the remaining gapless carrier modes. This provides a powerful, field-tunable transport diagnostic for characterizing spin textures in correlated materials.
main_problem: The paper investigates carrier-mediated spin helices in low-dimensional systems, focusing on how these helices manifest in Josephson interference features and how they affect carrier correlations.
main_result: The study establishes that coupled-wire carrier-localized-spin systems exhibit RKKY-driven collective helical order, which can be detected via characteristic modifications in Josephson interference patterns and reconstructed carrier-sector signatures.
method: The analysis employs a combination of bosonization techniques, variational treatments, and theoretical modeling of anisotropic Superconductor-Normal-metal-Superconductor (SNS) Josephson junctions.
model_or_system: The models include interacting one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) coupled-wire systems, such as those mimicking twisted bilayer WTe2. The physics is described using Luttinger liquid theory, incorporating carrier-localized spin interactions.
key_observables: Josephson interference features (central-lobe width, side-lobe asymmetry), gap reconstruction in the carrier sector, and correlation exponents ($\chi_c^n(r)$, $\chi_s^\mu{}_n(r)$).
important_parameters: Applied in-plane magnetic field, coupling strengths, and the dimensionality (1D vs. 2D) of the coupled wires.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on low-energy effective theories, bosonization, and variational approximations for gap estimation.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the text describes analyzing modifications to Josephson interference patterns and reconstructed local-density-of-states exponents.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the theory by first introducing the four classes of coupled 1D/2D systems, then developing the RKKY interaction and helical order, followed by analyzing the Josephson interference signatures, and finally examining the reconstructed carrier-sector observables.
why_interesting: The connection between collective magnetic order (helical spin texture) and measurable transport signatures (Josephson interference) in low-dimensional correlated electron systems is highly relevant to understanding exotic superconducting and magnetic phases in modern 2D materials.
